extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, university tech-transfer offices, federal agency contracting officers, inventors, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing patent rights, filing, licensing, and agency/regulatory duties for inventions made under federal funding agreements (Chapter 18, 35 U.S.C.). Covers contractor elections, march-in rights, confidentiality, licensing criteria, and related definitions and penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing prohibition (35 U.S.C. 184)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except when authorized by a license obtained from the Commissioner of Patents a person shall not file or cause or authorize to be filed in any foreign country prior to six months after filing in the United States an application for patent or for the registration of a utility model, industrial design, or model in respect of an invention made in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license may be granted retroactively where an application has been filed abroad through error and without deceptive intent and the application does not disclose an invention within the scope of section 181. The scope of a license shall permit subsequent modifications, amendments, and supplements containing additional subject matter if the U.S. application was not required to be made available for inspection under section 181 and such changes do not change the general nature of the invention in a manner that would require disclosure under section 181. The term “application” includes applications and any modifications, amendments, or supplements thereto, or divisions thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent barred for filing without license (35 U.S.C. 185)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person shall not receive a United States patent for an invention if that person, without procuring the license prescribed in section 184, has made, or consented to or assisted another’s making, application in a foreign country for a patent or registration in respect of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A U.S. patent issued to such person shall be invalid unless the failure to procure such license was through error (and in some pre-AIA text also 'without deceptive intent') and the patent does not disclose subject matter within the scope of section 181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for willful disclosure or foreign filing (35 U.S.C. 186)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever, during the period an invention has been ordered to be kept secret and the grant of a patent withheld pursuant to section 181, with knowledge of such order and without due authorization, willfully publish or disclose the invention, or whoever willfully, in violation of section 184, files in any foreign country an application for patent shall, upon conviction, be fined not more than $10,000 or imprisoned for not more than two years, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal penalty requires willful action and knowledge of the secrecy order or willful violation of foreign-filing prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from prohibitions (35 U.S.C. 187)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibitions and penalties of this chapter shall not apply to any officer or agent of the United States acting within the scope of his authority, nor to any person acting upon his written instructions or permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts taken pursuant to official written instruction or within the scope of authority are carved out from the chapter's filing and disclosure prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency rulemaking and delegation (35 U.S.C. 188)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atomic Energy Commission, the Secretary of a defense department, the chief officer of any other department or agency designated by the President as a defense agency, and the Secretary of Commerce, may separately issue rules and regulations to enable the respective department or agency to carry out the provisions of this chapter, and may delegate any power conferred by this chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorizes agencies to adopt implementing regulations and to delegate powers needed to enforce secrecy, foreign filing controls, and related functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and objective (35 U.S.C. 200)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the policy and objective of the Congress to use the patent system to promote the utilization of inventions arising from federally supported research or development; to encourage maximum participation of small business firms in federally supported research and development efforts; to promote collaboration between commercial concerns and nonprofit organizations; to ensure inventions by nonprofit organizations and small businesses are used to promote competition and not unduly encumber future research; to promote commercialization and public availability; to ensure the Government obtains sufficient rights to meet its needs and protect the public; and to minimize administrative costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory policy frames how dispositions of rights, licensing, and agency actions should be evaluated and implemented under Chapter 18 (commonly known as Bayh–Dole policy objectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions (35 U.S.C. 201)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key terms defined: 'Federal agency' (executive agency + military departments); 'funding agreement' (contract, grant, cooperative agreement for research/development funded in whole or part by the Federal Government, including assignments/subcontracts); 'contractor' (person, small business firm, or nonprofit organization party to a funding agreement); 'invention' (invention or discovery patentable under this title or novel plant variety); 'subject invention' (any invention of the contractor conceived or first actually reduced to practice in performance of work under a funding agreement); 'practical application' (manufacture, practice, or operation under conditions showing invention is utilized and benefits available to public on reasonable terms); 'made' (conception or first actual reduction to practice); 'small business firm' and 'nonprofit organization' defined by statute and IRS sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions determine what inventions and activities fall under Chapter 18 obligations (e.g., what counts as a subject invention, what constitutes practical application, and who is a contractor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor election to retain title; exceptions (35 U.S.C. 202(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each nonprofit organization or small business firm may, within a reasonable time after disclosure, elect to retain title to any subject invention: Provided, however, That a funding agreement may provide otherwise (i) when the contractor is not located in the United States or does not have a place of business in the United States or is subject to the control of a foreign government, (ii) in exceptional circumstances where the agency determines restriction/elimination better promotes policy, (iii) when authorized to protect foreign intelligence/counterintelligence activities, or (iv) when the funding agreement includes operation of a Government-owned contractor-operated DOE facility dedicated to naval nuclear propulsion or weapons-related programs (with specified limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractor election is the norm but agencies may withhold or limit election rights in narrowly specified situations; rights retained by contractors remain subject to the statutory provisions and agency regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency determinations and oversight (35 U.S.C. 202(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of the Government under subsection (a) shall not be exercised by a Federal agency unless it first determines that at least one of the conditions in (a)(i)-(iii) exists. Except for (a)(iii), the agency shall file with the Secretary of Commerce, within thirty days after award of the funding agreement, a copy of such determination; determinations under (a)(ii) must include an analysis justifying the determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of Commerce may review and advise; Office of Federal Procurement Policy Administrator may issue regulations describing improper agency uses of these authorities. Contractors may challenge determinations under section 203(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required funding agreement provisions (35 U.S.C. 202(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each funding agreement with a small business firm or nonprofit organization shall contain appropriate provisions to effectuate specific obligations: (1) disclosure of each subject invention to the Federal agency within a reasonable time; (2) written election within two years after disclosure whether contractor will retain title (or such additional agency-approved time); (3) contractor agreeing to file a patent application prior to statutory bar dates and corresponding foreign filings within reasonable times; (4) agency’s nonexclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license to practice the subject invention worldwide; (5) agency’s right to require periodic reporting on utilization or efforts to obtain utilization (treated as confidential commercial/financial information); (6) obligation to include a statement in patent specifications that invention was made with Government support and Government has certain rights; (7) nonprofit-specific obligations including prohibition on assignment of U.S. rights without agency approval (with exceptions), requirement to share royalties with inventors, requirement to use royalty balances for research/education (with specified exceptions), preference in licensing given to small business firms, and special rules for Government-owned-contractor-operated facilities; and (8) the requirements of sections 203 and 204.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeframes: disclosure 'within a reasonable time', election generally within two years (with agency adjustments for statutory bars), and filing 'prior to any statutory bar date.' Failure to meet disclosure/election/filing obligations can lead to the Government receiving title. Reporting and confidentiality protections apply to utilization data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government title if contractor fails to elect or file (35 U.S.C. 202(c) cross-references)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Government may receive title to any subject invention in which the contractor does not elect to retain rights or fails to elect rights within the required times; similarly, the Government may receive title to subject inventions in countries where the contractor has not filed patent applications within reasonable times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may shorten election periods when a statutory one-year patent bar is triggered by publication, sale, or public use; contractors must coordinate election and timely filing to avoid loss of title to the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may grant inventor retention requests (35 U.S.C. 202(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contractor does not elect to retain title to a subject invention in cases subject to this section, the Federal agency may consider and after consultation with the contractor grant requests for retention of rights by the inventor subject to the provisions of this Act and regulations promulgated hereunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors may, under certain conditions, obtain retention of rights if the contractor declines to elect title; agency exercises discretionary authority and must follow statute/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal employee coinventor consolidation (35 U.S.C. 202(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Federal employee is a coinventor with a contractor, the Federal agency employing such coinventor may, to consolidate rights and if it finds that doing so would expedite development, license or assign whatever rights it may acquire to the contractor or acquire rights from the contractor, but only voluntarily and not conditioned on other transactions under the chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits consolidation of rights to expedite commercialization but requires voluntary transactions and agency findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on requiring third-party licensing of non-subject inventions (35 U.S.C. 202(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: No funding agreement with a small business firm or nonprofit organization shall contain a provision allowing a Federal agency to require licensing to third parties of inventions owned by the contractor that are not subject inventions unless such provision has been approved by the head of the agency with a written justification. Any such provision shall clearly state whether licensing may be required in connection with the practice of a subject invention, a specifically identified work object, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The head of the agency may not delegate approval authority. The agency may not require licensing under such a provision unless it determines on the record and after hearing that use by others is necessary for the practice of a subject invention or to achieve practical application, and judicial review must be brought within sixty days after notification of such determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: March-in rights triggers (35 U.S.C. 203(a)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A Federal agency has the right to require the contractor, an assignee, or exclusive licensee of a subject invention to grant a license to responsible applicants or to grant the license itself if it determines that: (1) the contractor/assignee has not taken, or is not expected to take within a reasonable time, effective steps to achieve practical application of the invention; (2) action is necessary to alleviate health or safety needs not reasonably satisfied by contractor/assignee/licensees; (3) action is necessary to meet requirements for public use specified by Federal regulations and such requirements are not reasonably satisfied; or (4) action is necessary because the agreement required by section 204 has not been obtained or waived or because a licensee is in breach of its agreement obtained pursuant to section 204.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: March-in is a statutory remedy to ensure practical application and public welfare; 'practical application' and 'reasonable time' are fact-specific determinations made under agency procedures and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: March-in appeals and abeyance (35 U.S.C. 203(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination under this section shall have administrative appeals procedures established by regulation; any adversely affected party may, within sixty days, file a petition in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims to review the determination on the record. In cases under paragraphs (1) and (3) of subsection (a), the agency’s determination shall be held in abeyance pending exhaustion of appeals or petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides judicial review rights and mandates abeyance for certain march-in determinations while appeals proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for United States industry (35 U.S.C. 204)
rubrics_metrics.description: No small business firm or nonprofit organization that receives title to any subject invention, nor any assignee, shall grant the exclusive right to use or sell the subject invention in the U.S. unless the licensee agrees that products embodying the subject invention or produced through its use will be manufactured substantially in the United States. The requirement may be waived by the Federal agency upon showing reasonable but unsuccessful efforts to grant licenses to potential licensees likely to manufacture substantially in the U.S. or that domestic manufacture is not commercially feasible under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard imposes a domestic manufacture preference for exclusive licenses; waivers available upon adequate showing to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality authority for agency-held invention information (35 U.S.C. 205)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies are authorized to withhold from disclosure to the public information disclosing any invention in which the Federal Government owns or may own a right for a reasonable time in order for a patent application to be filed; agencies are not required to release copies of any document which is part of an application for patent filed with the USPTO or foreign patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits agencies to protect patentable subject matter information from public disclosure to preserve patent rights and filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of Commerce: uniform clauses and standard regulations (35 U.S.C. 206)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of Commerce may issue regulations applicable to Federal agencies implementing sections 202 through 204 and shall establish standard funding agreement provisions required under this chapter; the regulations and standard funding agreement shall be subject to public comment before issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizes rulemaking and standard clause formulation at Commerce and requires public comment before issuance, promoting uniformity across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authority for domestic and foreign protection of federally owned inventions (35 U.S.C. 207)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Federal agency is authorized to apply for, obtain, and maintain patents or other forms of protection in the United States and foreign countries on inventions in which the Federal Government owns a right, to grant nonexclusive, exclusive, or partially exclusive licenses (royalty-free or for royalties) on such terms as appropriate, to undertake other steps to protect and administer rights to federally owned inventions (including acquiring rights for and administering royalties), and to transfer custody and administration of rights to another Federal agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants agencies broad authority to protect, license, and manage federally owned inventions domestically and abroad; includes authority to transfer custody/administration among agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations governing Federal licensing (35 U.S.C. 208)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of Commerce is authorized to promulgate regulations specifying the terms and conditions upon which any federally owned invention (other than those owned by the TVA) may be licensed on a nonexclusive, partially exclusive, or exclusive basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce sets licensing regulatory framework for federally owned inventions to ensure consistent licensing practices across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for granting exclusive or partially exclusive licenses of federally owned inventions (35 U.S.C. 209)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Federal agency may grant an exclusive or partially exclusive license on a federally owned invention only if: (1) granting the license is a reasonable and necessary incentive to call forth investment capital or otherwise promote utilization; (2) the agency finds the public will be served by the grant as indicated by the applicant’s intentions, plans, and ability to bring the invention to practical application and that the proposed exclusivity is not greater than reasonably necessary; (3) the applicant commits to achieve practical application within a reasonable time (time may be extended by the agency upon request and justification); (4) granting the license will not tend to substantially lessen competition or create/maintain an antitrust violation; and (5) for inventions covered by foreign applications or patents, the interests of the Federal Government or U.S. industry in foreign commerce will be enhanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional statutory conditions: (b) normally grant licenses only to licensees agreeing that products will be manufactured substantially in the U.S.; (c) first preference to small businesses with equal/greater likelihood of bringing invention to practical application; (d) licenses shall contain terms the agency considers appropriate and must retain an irrevocable, paid-up license for the Government to practice the invention worldwide.
